[Information, geometry & gravity]{.eyebrow}

::: {.page-intro}
I study multipartite entanglement in holography, developing measures of quantum correlations shared among several subsystems and understanding their geometric descriptions. In a separate direction, I construct new black hole solutions in AdS/CFT and study their thermodynamics and phase transitions, including configurations with charge or angular momentum outside the horizon.
:::

## Quantum Information in Quantum Gravity {#quantum-information}

### From two subsystems to many {#entanglement}

Entanglement entropy measures quantum correlations across a division into two parts. In a pure state with three or more subsystems, there are additional ways for correlations to be shared. Grouping parties together can hide this structure: the entropies of individual subsystems need not capture every invariant of the full state. My work develops measures that treat the multiple parties together and asks how their algebraic structure appears in gravity.

The starting point is the replica method. For a bipartite system, copies of a reduced density matrix are joined cyclically, and the resulting contraction gives a Rényi entropy. The multi-entropy construction instead uses a lattice of replicas, with a separate cyclic permutation associated with each party. The resulting [Rényi multi-entropy](papers/2206.09723.qmd) is

$$
S^{({\mathtt{q}})}_{n}\equiv\frac{1}{1-n}{\rm Log}\,({\mathcal{Z}}_{n}^{({\mathtt{q}})}/({\mathcal{Z}}_{1}^{({\mathtt{q}})})^{n^{{\mathtt{q}}-1}}).
$$

Here $\mathtt{q}$ counts the parties, $n$ is the replica parameter, and $\mathcal{Z}^{(\mathtt{q})}_n$ is the specified contraction of copies of the state and its conjugate. The normalization removes dependence on the norm of the state. The construction reduces to the familiar Rényi entropy for two parties, while retaining information about more general multipartite correlations.

![Figure 1. A three-party state can be represented by a density matrix (left). Joining copies of this matrix in a periodic lattice (right) gives the contraction $\mathcal{Z}^{(3)}_4$ used to define multi-entropy. The lattice labels replicas of the state. ([arXiv:2206.09723](https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.09723))](assets/papers/2206.09723/rho3.svg){fig-alt="The three-party density matrix and the replica contraction used to define multi-entropy."}

Continuing the replica parameter toward one defines multi-entropy itself:

$$
S^{({\mathtt{q}})}={\rm lim}_{n\to{1}}\,S^{({\mathtt{q}})}_{n}.
$$

This continuation relates the integer-replica contractions to a continuous entropy-like quantity. A related question is how these quantities change when two parties are merged. Work on the [monotonicity conjecture](papers/2308.16247.qmd) proves particular cases and develops evidence for others, while leaving the general statement conjectural.

### Replica symmetry and bulk geometry {#holography}

In holography, a quantum field theory admits a gravitational description in one higher dimension. Ordinary entanglement entropy is encoded by an extremal area. The multipartite problem suggests a richer structure: networks of surfaces that partition the bulk into chambers, with junctions where surfaces meet. The replica construction determines the gluing of boundary regions; a compatible bulk saddle must implement that gluing geometrically.

![Figure 2. Boundary regions $\mathcal{R}_{\mathtt a}$ are associated with bulk chambers $\mathcal{C}_{\mathtt a}$. The walls separating neighboring chambers form a network of surfaces, with labels fixed by the replica permutations of the adjacent regions. ([arXiv:2304.06082](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.06082))](assets/papers/2304.06082/setup.svg){fig-alt="Boundary regions and bulk chambers separated by a network of walls."}

The [classification program](papers/2304.06082.qmd) studies more general permutation contractions and the finite groups organizing their replica symmetries. The subsequent [bulk replica symmetry analysis](papers/2411.00935.qmd) asks when those symmetries can extend to a smooth covering geometry. This constrains which proposed networks admit a symmetric gravitational realization. The goal is to identify the quantum observables and the geometric assumptions required for each correspondence, including the possibility that a dominant saddle breaks replica symmetry.

## Black Holes and Holography {#black-holes}

### Black holes with charge outside the horizon

In anti-de Sitter space, a black hole can share its conserved charges with matter outside its horizon. I study such configurations in AdS/CFT and determine which phase has the largest entropy at fixed energy, charge, and angular momentum. The resulting phase diagrams describe new equilibrium states of the dual quantum field theory.

A central example is a **dual dressed black hole**: a black-hole core surrounded by a small number of large dual giant gravitons. These expanded branes carry electric charge, while the core supplies the leading entropy. The [charged-superradiance study](papers/2409.18178.qmd) constructs these configurations in $AdS_5\times S^5$ and analyzes how they arise when a charged black hole becomes unstable. Entropy maximization determines how the total charge is divided between the core and its dressing.

**Grey galaxies** provide a rotational counterpart, with angular momentum carried by a distant gas. Together, charged and rotational dressing extend the supersymmetric ground-state phases beyond the family of isolated black holes. In the [two-charge $AdS_4$ analysis](papers/2510.16274.qmd), supersymmetric states saturate the energy bound

$$
E\ell\geq J+2(Q_{1}\ell+Q_{2}\ell)~.
$$

Here $\ell$ is the AdS radius, $E$ is energy, $J$ is angular momentum, and $Q_1,Q_2$ are electric charges. Regular single-center supersymmetric black holes satisfy a further nonlinear charge relation, forming a surface in charge space. Combining a core with an additional gas produces distinct phases on either side of that surface.

![Figure 3. Supersymmetric single-center black holes lie on a curved sheet in the space of electric-charge densities and angular momentum. The translucent foreground shows where the sheet folds over into a second branch. Configurations containing a core and a gas extend the phase diagram beyond this sheet. ([arXiv:2510.16274](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.16274))](assets/papers/2510.16274/bhsheet.png){fig-alt="The supersymmetric black-hole sheet, with its folded branch visible through the translucent foreground."}

### Phase transitions and the superconformal index

The superconformal index is a protected, signed count of quantum states. Its charge combinations group states along lines in charge space. A new dressed configuration can dominate the leading entropy on such a line, changing the phase predicted for the index. In the [grey-galaxy and index study](papers/2501.17217.qmd), an entropy-maximization prescription, together with the unobstructed saddle conjecture, predicts nine index phases. The numerical index provides an independent test of those predictions.

![Figure 4. Numerical index entropy at $N=10$ (red points) is compared with the single-black-hole prediction (blue) and the grey-galaxy prediction (orange), as the angular-momentum imbalance $j_R$ varies at fixed index-charge combination. The combined solid curve follows the black-hole branch before changing to the grey-galaxy branch, matching the trend in the numerical data. ([arXiv:2501.17217](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.17217))](assets/papers/2501.17217/N10GG.svg){fig-alt="Red numerical index data compared with blue single-black-hole and orange grey-galaxy entropy predictions."}

The change from the blue branch to the orange branch is a direct signature of the proposed phase transition. The finite-$N$ data follow the trend expected from the leading large-$N$ calculation, showing how configurations with matter outside the horizon change the microscopic count. The distinction between entropy at fixed charges and the signed index is central to this comparison.

I also study the Euclidean gravitational description of these transitions. Supersymmetric black holes contribute complex saddles to the path integral. The [complex-black-hole analysis](papers/2602.05979.qmd) applies the Kontsevich–Segal–Witten criterion to this family and finds that geometric admissibility tracks the convergence region of the boundary index. This supplies a gravitational diagnostic for the onset of grey-galaxy physics.
